name: Drainage basins & the continental divide
scope: The invisible ridge-lines that decide which ocean a raindrop reaches. T1: along the Continental Divide of the Americas — the crest of the Rocky Mountains — rain landing on the west side runs to the Pacific and rain on the east side runs (via the Gulf of Mexico) to the Atlantic; the ridge sorts every drop. T2: at Triple Divide Peak in Montana's Glacier National Park, meltwater from ONE summit can set off for three different seas — the Pacific, the Atlantic (Gulf of Mexico), and Hudson Bay toward the Arctic — a rare 'hydrological apex.' T3: the Amazon basin drains about 7 million km2 — roughly 40% of the entire South American continent — the largest drainage basin on Earth (invert the wonder: the giant basin is the hook, 'the Amazon' the answer). T4: the Casiquiare in Venezuela is a natural 'bifurcation' — a river that branches off the upper Orinoco and flows into the Rio Negro, secretly linking the Orinoco and Amazon basins that are supposed to be separate. T5: divides can move — 'river capture' (stream piracy), where a fast-cutting stream beheads a neighbor and steals its headwaters; geologists think the Casiquiare is slowly capturing more of the upper Orinoco this way. Distractors: other real divides/basins (the Congo basin, the Mississippi basin, Australia's Great Dividing Range).
source: Wikipedia: Casiquiare canal (fetched, corroborated bifurcation Orinoco<->Rio Negro/Amazon & slow stream-capture); Amazon River (fetched: ~7M km2 basin, largest); plus canonical pages to research at build (Grokipedia-first per PIPELINE, corroborate Wikipedia): Continental Divide of the Americas, Triple Divide Peak, Drainage divide.
framing_note: PLACE in every stem (a named ridge, peak, or basin); the answer is which ocean the water reaches, or the named divide/bifurcation — never a bare number. Teach 'drainage basin/watershed' and 'continental divide' before testing. Invert on T3 (basin size -> 'the Amazon'). Dinner-test payoff: Triple Divide Peak (one snowflake, three seas) and the Casiquiare (a river that cheats by belonging to two basins). Distractors are other real divides/basins so all four choices stay live. Pure earth-process — no food/animal content.

name: The world's great rivers
scope: The planet's mightiest rivers, each keyed to a knowable named fact rather than a bare superlative. T1: the Nile (~6,650 km) runs the 'wrong' way — south to north, out of the heart of Africa to the Mediterranean — and its floods built ancient Egypt. T2: the Amazon carries about a FIFTH (20%) of all the water the world's rivers deliver to the oceans, more than the next several biggest rivers combined (the discharge is the hook, 'the Amazon' the answer). T3: the Blue Nile pours off the Ethiopian Highlands out of Lake Tana and delivers most of the Nile's flood, while the White Nile's remotest waters feed from the Lake Victoria region — a place-anchored 'where the Nile begins,' no bare date. T4: the Congo is the world's DEEPEST river, plunging to about 220 m in dark canyons where isolated fish evolved, and it is the only great river to cross the equator twice. T5: at the 'Meeting of the Waters' by Manaus the coffee-black Rio Negro and the sandy Solimoes run side by side for about 6 km WITHOUT mixing, because they differ in temperature, speed, and density. Extra rungs: the Yangtze (Asia's longest, the Three Gorges); the Danube (flows through more countries — about ten — than any other river); the Mississippi-Missouri (North America's great artery). Distractors: other great rivers.
source: Wikipedia: Amazon River (fetched: 20% of global riverine discharge, largest basin, Nile length dispute, Meeting of the Waters at Manaus); Congo River (fetched: deepest ~220 m, crosses equator twice, 3rd by discharge, Livingstone Falls). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Nile, Blue Nile, Yangtze, Danube.
framing_note: Invert every superlative (put the number in the stem, make the NAMED river the answer). Teach 'discharge/drainage' before testing. ACCURACY RAIL: the Congo is 3rd by discharge (behind the Amazon and Ganges-Brahmaputra) — word its rung as 'deepest,' never 'second-biggest.' Dinner-test payoff: the Meeting of the Waters (two rivers that refuse to blend) and the Congo's deep-canyon abyss. Distractors are other real rivers so all four stay live.
history_overlap: Ancient Egypt on the Nile, and the Victorian search for the Nile's source (Speke/Burton), may appear as human-history episodes in the history bank; keep every answer here a river/landscape fact, not a dated human event.

name: Endorheic basins — water with no way out to the sea
scope: Places where water flows IN and only evaporation takes it out, so the salt piles up. T1: the Dead Sea lies about 430 m BELOW sea level — the lowest dry land on Earth — and is so salty (roughly ten times the ocean) that a swimmer bobs like a cork; the Jordan River feeds it but nothing drains out. T2: the Caspian Sea is the world's LARGEST lake — bigger than all five North American Great Lakes combined — yet it reaches no ocean, losing water only to the sky (invert: the giant size is the hook, 'a closed sea with no outlet' the answer). T3: Utah's Great Salt Lake is the shrunken remnant of Ice-Age Lake Bonneville; where it dried it left the dead-flat, blinding-white Bonneville Salt Flats, hard enough to set world land-speed records on. T4: the Aral Sea was the world's fourth-largest lake until, from the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the Amu Darya and Syr Darya to irrigate cotton; the sea collapsed into the toxic 'Aralkum' desert, stranding rusting fishing ships tens of kilometers from any water. T5: the Okavango River in Botswana never reaches the sea at all — it spreads into the Kalahari as a huge inland delta that pulses green in the dry season and then vanishes into sand. Extra rungs: Salar de Uyuni (Bolivia), the ~10,000 km2 salt-flat 'mirror' left by dried paleolakes; the Great Basin of the U.S. (no drop reaches an ocean); the shrinking of Lake Chad. Distractors: other salt/closed lakes and salt flats.
source: Wikipedia: Aral Sea (fetched: Soviet Amu Darya/Syr Darya diversion for cotton from the 1960s, once 4th-largest lake, Aralkum desert, stranded boats at Moynaq). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Dead Sea, Caspian Sea, Great Salt Lake / Lake Bonneville, Okavango Delta, Salar de Uyuni, Endorheic basin.
framing_note: Teach 'endorheic (no outlet to the sea)' before testing. Every answer is a place-fact (why it's salty / lowest / dried), never a bare number. VISION-MANDATED on the Aral rung: name the Soviet cotton diversion plainly as the cause — honest environmental record written on the land, active voice (planners diverted the rivers), no euphemism. Dinner-test payoff: the Aral's ships stranded in the desert, and floating on the Dead Sea. Lane border: the WILDLIFE of these basins (Caspian sturgeon, Okavango game) is the animal bank — keep the answer the landform/hydrology (inland delta, no outlet, salt flat), never a creature. Distractors are other real closed lakes.

name: The meander & the oxbow lake
scope: How a river wanders across its own valley and then strangles its own bends. T1: on the lower Mississippi the river swings in giant S-curves called meanders — fast and biting on the outside of each bend, slow and depositing on the inside. T2: when a loop grows so tight that a flood cuts straight across its neck, the abandoned bend is left behind as a crescent 'oxbow lake' — the Mississippi valley is freckled with them (name the landform = the answer). T3: at the Goosenecks of the San Juan River in Utah the river coils back on itself in tight loops 300 m below the desert floor — 'entrenched (incised) meanders,' bends the river sawed DOWNWARD into solid rock as the whole land rose, so it could no longer wander free (invert: the 300 m depth is the hook). T4: Horseshoe Bend near Page, Arizona, is a single incised meander of the Colorado — the green river wrapped almost all the way around a lone sandstone butte. T5: 'The Rincon' on the Colorado is an ABANDONED incised meander: ages ago the river cut across the neck and walked away, leaving a dry, rock-walled loop stranded high above the new channel — a fossil oxbow carved in stone. Distractors: other river landforms (delta, canyon, waterfall, braided channel).
source: Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Meander, Oxbow lake, Goosenecks State Park / San Juan River, Horseshoe Bend (Arizona), Incised meander, The Rincon (Colorado River).
framing_note: Teach 'meander,' 'oxbow lake,' and 'incised/entrenched meander' before testing; every answer is a named landform or a named place. Invert on T3 (the 300 m depth -> 'entrenched meander'). Dinner-test payoff: the oxbow lake (a river that strangles its own bend) and the Rincon (a canyon-loop the river abandoned). Pure geomorphology — no animal/food. Distractors are adjacent real river features so all four stay live.

name: River deltas — where a river drops its load
scope: The fans of new land a river builds where it finally meets still water. T1: where the Nile hits the Mediterranean it splays into a green triangle so like the Greek letter Delta that the ancient Greeks named the whole landform after it — the Nile Delta, ancient Egypt's breadbasket. T2: the Mississippi doesn't fan — it pokes long skinny fingers into the Gulf of Mexico, a 'bird's-foot' delta, built where the river dumps mud faster than the sea can sweep it away. T3: the Ganges and Brahmaputra together build the LARGEST delta on Earth, the Bengal delta, whose seaward fringe is the Sundarbans, the world's biggest tidal mangrove forest (the answer is the delta/Sundarbans landform, not the tiger). T4: the Danube Delta on the Black Sea is Europe's largest and best-preserved wetland — a maze of reed channels where the river is still adding new land each year. T5: a delta is a tug-of-war between a river building land and the sea plus the delta's own sinking weight tearing it down — starved of mud by upstream dams and levees, the Mississippi delta is now LOSING Louisiana wetland to the Gulf as it subsides. Extra rungs: the Lena Delta, a frozen Arctic fan in Siberia; a cross-reference to the Okavango, a river that 'deltas' into a desert instead of a sea. Distractors: other named deltas and river landforms.
source: Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Nile Delta, Mississippi River Delta, Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta / Sundarbans, Danube Delta, Lena Delta, River delta.
framing_note: Teach 'delta' and that its SHAPE depends on river mud vs. wave/tide power (fan vs. bird's-foot vs. tidal). Every answer is a named delta or its landform/shape. Invert on T3 (largest -> Ganges-Brahmaputra/Sundarbans). Dinner-test payoff: the bird's-foot delta and the disappearing-Louisiana rung. Lane border: the Sundarbans' tigers and wildlife are the animal bank; a delta city's cuisine is the cooking bank — keep every answer the delta landform. Distractors are other real deltas so all four stay live.

name: Tower karst — stone forests and drowned dragons
scope: Limestone hills dissolved by rain into forests of stone, above water and below it. T1: along the Li River around Guilin and Yangshuo, hundreds of steep limestone hills rise straight out of the flat rice paddies like a forest of green thumbs — 'tower karst,' rock slowly eaten by rainwater over millions of years. T2: the most famous stretch of that scenery, the peaks near Xingping on the Li River, is the very view printed on China's 20-yuan banknote (which real place is on the money = the answer). T3: teach the terms — a 'peak forest' of separate towers standing on a plain is fenglin; clustered cones sharing one base are fengcong; both are carved DOWN by water, not pushed UP by tectonics. T4: Ha Long Bay in Vietnam is DROWNED tower karst — the same limestone towers, but the sea rose and flooded the valleys between them, leaving about 1,600 islands jutting from the Gulf of Tonkin (invert: the 1,600-island hook -> drowned karst). T5: in Yunnan's Stone Forest (Shilin), rain dissolved the limestone from the top down into a maze of tall grey blades and pinnacles you can walk between — karst at ground level instead of towering hills. Distractors: other karst/rock scenery (fjords, mesas, hoodoos, and the Zhangjiajie sandstone pillars).
source: Wikipedia: Karst (fetched: definition, tower karst, dissolution). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Guilin / Li River, Yangshuo, Ha Long Bay, Stone Forest (Shilin), Tower karst (fenglin/fengcong).
framing_note: Teach 'karst' and 'tower karst / fenglin / fengcong' before testing; every stem names a real place and every answer is that place's landform or the term for it. Invert where possible (Ha Long's 1,600 islands -> drowned karst). Dinner-test payoff: the 20-yuan-note view and Ha Long as a flooded stone forest. ACCURACY RAIL: Zhangjiajie's pillars are QUARTZ SANDSTONE, not karst — use them as a distractor, never label them karst. Pure landform — no animal/food. Distractors keep all four choices live.

name: Cenotes — sinkholes to a flooded underworld
scope: The Yucatan's windows into the water hidden under the limestone. T1: the Yucatan Peninsula has almost NO rivers on its surface — rain sinks straight through the porous limestone — so the Maya drank from cenotes: natural wells where the cave roof collapsed and exposed the cool groundwater below. T2: the Maya believed a cenote was a doorway to Xibalba, the watery underworld; at the Sacred Cenote of Chichen Itza, divers and dredges later recovered jade, gold, and human remains — offerings cast in to petition Chaac, the rain god. T3: seen from the air, the peninsula's densest RING of cenotes traces a huge buried arc — the rim of the Chicxulub crater, the ~66-million-year-old scar of the asteroid impact tied to the dinosaurs' extinction; the cenotes line up over its fractured edge (invert: the mysterious ring -> the buried crater). T4: the flooded caves behind the cenotes join into the LONGEST underwater cave system on Earth — Sistema Sac Actun near Tulum, over 370 km of submerged passage mapped by cave divers. T5: nearby El Zacaton is the world's deepest known water-filled sinkhole, a flooded pit over 300 m deep, so hard to reach that NASA tested an autonomous diving robot in it. Extra rungs: a 'how a cenote forms' rung; the Dos Ojos / Ik Kil cenotes as named examples. Distractors: other water features (a spring, a lava tube, a blue hole — Belize's Great Blue Hole is an apt adjacent distractor).
source: Wikipedia: Cenote (fetched: limestone-collapse formation, Ring of Cenotes over the Chicxulub crater rim, Sacred Cenote offerings to Chaac, Xibalba portal belief, Sistema Sac Actun >376 km). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Chicxulub crater, El Zacaton, Sistema Sac Actun.
framing_note: Teach 'cenote' and 'sinkhole/collapse.' Every answer is a place-fact (the well, the underworld belief, the crater ring, the longest underwater cave, the deepest sinkhole). VISION-MANDATED: treat the Maya's sacred cenote and Xibalba with respect on their own terms — state the offerings plainly, no smug 'they merely thought,' no gore-tourism. Dinner-test payoff: the Ring of Cenotes tracing the dinosaur-killer crater. Lane border: the Maya CIVILIZATION as a human story belongs to the history bank — keep answers here place- and water-anchored. Distractors are adjacent real water features.
history_overlap: The Maya civilization and Chichen Itza as a human-history episode may live in the history bank; keep every answer here anchored to the cenote/water/crater (the well, the crater ring, the underwater cave), not to Maya political history.

name: Classic karst — the land that named itself
scope: The bare Slovenian plateau that gave geography one of its words, and the plumbing hidden beneath it. T1: on the stony Kras (Karst) plateau above the Adriatic, rain sinks into the limestone instead of running off in streams — a landscape so distinctive that scientists borrowed its very name, 'karst,' for every place on Earth that behaves this way (teach the term through its birthplace). T2: the Reka River flows across the surface and then simply VANISHES underground into the Skocjan Caves, thundering through one of the largest underground river canyons in the world before it disappears into the dark. T3: that lost river isn't gone — it runs unseen through the rock for tens of kilometers and RESURGES as the Timavo springs near the coast by Trieste, bursting back into daylight close to the sea. T4: a polje is a flat-floored karst plain that turns into a lake and back into a meadow with the seasons — Lake Cerknica in Slovenia fills in the wet season and drains away through swallow-holes in summer, an 'intermittent lake.' T5: teach the karst toolkit — a doline (sinkhole) is a closed pit that drains underground; a ponor (swallow-hole) gulps a whole stream; a resurgence spits it back out — a whole land plumbed by dissolved rock instead of surface rivers. Distractors: other landforms/processes (glacial valleys, volcanic craters, coastal features).
source: Wikipedia: Karst (fetched: etymology from the Kras/Karst plateau, polje, doline/sinkhole, sinking rivers, karst springs/resurgence). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Skocjan Caves, Reka River / Timavo, Lake Cerknica, Postojna Cave.
framing_note: This is the vocabulary ladder — teach 'karst,' 'polje,' 'doline/sinkhole,' 'ponor/resurgence,' the terms the tower-karst and cenote ladders lean on. Every stem names a real place (Kras, Skocjan, Timavo, Cerknica). Invert on T2 (a river that disappears -> the Skocjan swallow). Dinner-test payoff: the Reka/Timavo river that vanishes and reappears, and the lake that comes and goes. Lane border: Postojna's blind cave 'baby dragon' (the olm) is the animal bank — if Postojna appears, key the CAVE, not the amphibian. Distractors keep all four live.

name: The great caves — water's underground cathedrals
scope: The record-holding voids that seeping water has dissolved out of solid rock. T1: under the hills of Kentucky, Mammoth Cave is the LONGEST cave system in the world — over 686 km (426 miles) of surveyed passages already mapped and still growing — all eaten out of limestone by percolating water. T2: Son Doong in Vietnam holds the largest cave passage on Earth — roomy enough for a Boeing 747; where its ceiling collapsed, sunlight pours in and a jungle grows underground, and the cave even brews its own drifting clouds. T3: in New Mexico, Lechuguilla Cave was carved the 'wrong' way — from the BOTTOM UP, by sulfuric acid rising from deep oil deposits — and it is hung with 6-meter gypsum chandeliers found almost nowhere else (invert: acid-from-below is the hook, Lechuguilla the answer). T4: the two deepest caves ever found both plunge more than 2 km straight down into the Arabika Massif in Abkhazia — Veryovkina and Krubera(-Voronya) — vertical labyrinths that take divers weeks and have cost lives to reach the bottom of. T5: teach the difference — most caves grow slowly downward as rainwater turns mildly acidic and dissolves limestone (Mammoth, Carlsbad), but Lechuguilla's acid rose UP from oil below ('hypogene' cave-making), which is why its crystals are so bizarre. Extra rungs: Carlsbad Caverns' Big Room (key the chamber, not the bats); a 'how a limestone cave and its dripstone form' rung anchored to a named cave. Distractors: other named caves and cave types (lava tube, sea cave, ice cave).
source: Wikipedia (all fetched): Mammoth Cave National Park (>686 km / 426 mi, world's longest); Son Doong Cave (largest passage, 747-scale, dolines with jungle, own clouds, discovered by Ho Khanh 1990 / BCRA 2009, Phong Nha-Ke Bang); Lechuguilla Cave (hypogene sulfuric-acid formation from oil-derived H2S, gypsum chandeliers); Veryovkina Cave (>2 km deep, Arabika Massif, record vs. Krubera).
framing_note: Teach how dissolved limestone makes caves; every stem names a real cave and the answer is that cave's superlative made knowable (longest / biggest passage / acid-carved / deepest). ACCURACY RAIL on the deepest rung: state Veryovkina and Krubera as the TWO deepest (both >2 km, Arabika Massif) rather than betting on which is #1 — the record has swapped on re-survey. Invert wonders (the 747 hook -> Son Doong; acid-from-below -> Lechuguilla). Dinner-test payoff: Son Doong's jungle-and-clouds inside a cave, and Lechuguilla carved by acid rising from oil. Lane border: Carlsbad's bats and cave-adapted animals are the animal bank — key the cave/chamber. Distractors keep all four live.

name: Estuaries & tidal bores — where river meets the tide
scope: The mixing zones where a river's fresh water wrestles the sea's tide. T1: an estuary is where a river's fresh water meets and blends with the salty tide — like Chesapeake Bay, which is really the DROWNED valley of the Susquehanna River, flooded when the ice-age sea rose (a 'ria'). T2: in the funnel of Canada's Bay of Fundy the tide climbs about 16 m (52 ft) twice a day — the highest tides on Earth — enough that boats tied up at low tide sit on bare mud far below the docks (invert: the 16 m twice-a-day hook -> Bay of Fundy). T3: when a big incoming tide is squeezed into a narrowing river it can rear up into a single wave that races UPSTREAM — a tidal bore; the Qiantang River's 'Silver Dragon' in China is the world's largest, a wall of water up to ~9 m that crowds gather to watch each autumn. T4: on the Amazon a tidal bore called the pororoca rolls tens of kilometers up the river mouth — surfers ride a single wave for minutes (one rode it about 12 km for 37 minutes). T5: teach why bores happen — you need a huge tidal range AND a shallow, funnel-shaped, narrowing channel (the recipe behind the Severn bore in England as well as the Fundy and Qiantang giants); without the funnel the tide just rises quietly. Distractors: other coastal/river features (fjord, delta, lagoon, rip current).
source: Wikipedia: Bay of Fundy (fetched: highest tidal range, ~16 m, funnel resonance); Tidal bore (fetched: Qiantang 'Silver Dragon' up to ~9 m and largest, Amazon pororoca ~4 m and 37-min surf ride, Severn bore, funnel + >6 m tidal-range recipe). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Chesapeake Bay, Ria, Estuary.
framing_note: Teach 'estuary,' 'ria (drowned river valley),' and 'tidal bore' before testing; every stem names a real place. Invert on T2 (16 m twice a day -> Bay of Fundy). Dinner-test payoff: surfing the Amazon's pororoca and the Qiantang 'Silver Dragon.' ACCURACY NUANCE: Fundy's 'highest tides' claim is shared with Ungava Bay's Leaf Basin — say Fundy has the famous highest-average tidal range, don't over-claim a single global record. Pure hydrology — no animal/food. Distractors keep all four live.

name: Groundwater — the hidden rivers under our feet
scope: The vast unseen water in the rock — springs, aquifers, and rivers that run underground. T1: in the Palawan rainforest of the Philippines, the Puerto Princesa underground river flows for kilometers THROUGH a limestone mountain and out to the sea — you can take a boat into the dark along it (a navigable underground river). T2: most of the world's fresh LIQUID water isn't in rivers at all — it's groundwater, soaked into rock and sand below the surface; where that saturated rock (an 'aquifer') meets the ground it bursts out as a spring, like Florida's Silver Springs and Wakulla Springs, gushing crystal-clear from the limestone. T3: the Great Artesian Basin under eastern Australia is one of the largest groundwater basins on Earth — water that fell on distant highlands seeps for thousands of years and rises on its own at desert 'mound springs,' the only water for hundreds of dry kilometers (invert: what lets people survive the outback -> the artesian basin). T4: the Ogallala (High Plains) Aquifer waters much of the U.S. Great Plains, but it holds 'fossil' water banked since the Ice Age that barely refills — and in places pumping is drawing it down faster than a lifetime can replace it. T5: teach 'aquifer' and 'water table' — beneath the Sahara lies the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer, fossil water from a wetter age, which Libya pumped through the 'Great Man-Made River' pipelines to the coast: mining water that will not return. Distractors: other water sources (glacier, reservoir, desalination, a surface river).
source: Wikipedia: Puerto Princesa Subterranean River National Park (fetched: navigable underground river ~8.2 km flowing directly to the sea, limestone karst, UNESCO / New7Wonders). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Aquifer, Great Artesian Basin, Silver Springs (Florida) / Wakulla Springs, Ogallala Aquifer, Nubian Sandstone Aquifer / Great Man-Made River.
framing_note: This ladder covers the sub-strand's 'groundwater' explicitly — teach 'aquifer,' 'water table,' 'spring/artesian,' and 'fossil water.' Every stem names a real place (Puerto Princesa, Silver/Wakulla Springs, the Great Artesian Basin, the Ogallala, the Nubian aquifer). Invert on T3 (surviving the outback -> the artesian basin). Dinner-test payoff: a river you ride a boat INTO a mountain (Puerto Princesa), and 'fossil water' older than farming. The depletion rungs state facts plainly with no policy verdict. Pure hydrology/place. Distractors keep all four live.

name: Waterfalls — the river's great leaps
scope: Where a river meets a sudden drop, keyed to named places and the process behind them. T1: deep in Venezuela's Canaima wilderness, water falls 979 m off the edge of Auyan-tepui, a flat-topped 'table mountain' — so far that it drifts into mist before it lands: Angel Falls, the world's tallest uninterrupted waterfall (the Pemon call it Kerepakupai Vena). T2: on the Zambezi a curtain of water 1,708 m wide and about 108 m tall throws up spray visible for miles — locals named it Mosi-oa-Tunya, 'the smoke that thunders'; we call it Victoria Falls, the world's largest single SHEET of falling water. T3: Victoria Falls hides how it was made — the river carved a zigzag of deep gorges by tearing along cracks (fault lines) in the flat basalt, and the falls have marched slowly upstream, gorge by gorge, over the ages. T4: on the Argentina-Brazil border the Iguazu River shatters into about 275 separate falls in a great horseshoe; its deepest throat, the Devil's Throat (Garganta del Diablo), swallows half the river in one roaring U. T5: Niagara is neither the tallest nor the widest, but it is the classic lesson in how waterfalls MOVE — the hard cap-rock breaks off at the lip and the falls erode UPSTREAM (a retreating 'knickpoint'), which is why Niagara has crept kilometers up its gorge since the Ice Age. Extra rung: Boyoma/Inga Falls on the Congo, the largest waterfall by sheer volume of flow. Distractors: other named waterfalls (Niagara vs. Victoria vs. Angel vs. Iguazu vs. Tugela).
source: Wikipedia (fetched): Angel Falls (979 m, tallest uninterrupted, Auyan-tepui, Pemon name Kerepakupai Vena, Tugela Falls dispute); Victoria Falls (Mosi-oa-Tunya, 1,708 m wide x ~108 m, largest sheet of falling water, zigzag gorges along basalt fault lines). Build-research (Grokipedia-first, corroborate Wikipedia): Iguazu Falls, Niagara Falls, Boyoma/Inga Falls.
framing_note: Waterfalls are river features and belong in this sub-strand; teach 'tepui,' 'knickpoint/headward retreat,' and 'cataract.' Invert superlatives (the 979 m mist-before-it-lands hook -> Angel Falls; the 'largest sheet' -> Victoria). ACCURACY RAIL: Angel Falls' 'tallest' is contested with South Africa's Tugela Falls — say 'tallest uninterrupted' and note the rival; use indigenous names respectfully (Mosi-oa-Tunya, Kerepakupai Vena) alongside the European ones. Dinner-test payoff: water that turns to mist before it reaches the ground (Angel) and the Devil's Throat. Lane border: the tepui as a 'lost world' of endemic species is the animal/ecology bank, and Livingstone's naming of Victoria Falls is one-line context — keep every answer the waterfall/landform. Distractors keep all four live.
